newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban say they seize key airbase, Afghan town.
newsitem.headline: Taleban say they seize key airbase, Afghan town.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban militia captured a key military airbase and a town north of Kabul in a big offensive on Thursday, Taleban sources said.
The sources said Taleban fighters had seized Bagram airbase and the town of Charikar, about 50 km (30 miles) from the Afghan capital in heavy fighting.
A spokesman at Taleban headquarters in southern Kandahar city said its forces had captured 500 opposition fighters as they thrust north.
"We are now advancing north of Charikar," Sayed Mohammed Haqqani told the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP).
No independent account of the battle, which followed three days of inconclusive U.N.-sponsored peace talks between the Taleban and its opponents, was immediately available.
Wounded fighters on the Taleban side of the front line said both sides had suffered heavy casualties in the fighting.
"Bagram airbase was captured late this morning and Charikar city has also come under our control," said one fighter.
The Soviet-built airbase and Charikar had been held by the forces of former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood and his powerful ally, northern Uzbek General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
Taleban fighters at Mir Bacha Kot village about 30 km (19 miles) north of Kabul said they were moving on two fronts, along the so-called old and new roads to Bagram.
"We are advancing from two directions," one fighter said, adding that the attack had begun at 6 a.m. (0130 GMT).
Taleban jet fighters were bombing opposition-held areas, but it was not clear if they had scored any hits.
The fighting was the most intense on the front lines north of Kabul for about three weeks.
AIP reported earlier that at least 12 opposition fighters and three Taleban militiamen had been killed in the battle for Bagram, scene of the heaviest clashes.
It said seven Taleban fighters had been wounded in the two-pronged assault from the Qarabagh area to the south and the village of Bagram to the west of the battered airfield.
Bagram fell to the purist Taleban after they captured Kabul on September 27, but was retaken by Masood on October 18. The Taleban grabbed it back on December 27, but held it only for a few hours.
When opposition forces captured the base in October there were eight apparently useless fighter jets, several transport aircraft and helicopter carcasses on the tarmac.
The base, sitting on a dusty plain with snow-capped peaks in the background, was used by Soviet forces in the 1980s to support a communist-backed government in Kabul.
The latest fighting came a day after peace talks between the Taleban and its opponents ended in Islamabad.
The United Nations Special Mission to Afghanistan (UNSMA), headed by Norbert Holl, had organised the three-day meeting that grouped three representatives from each side.

UNSMA said on Wednesday the talks had reached agreement on several points, including the urgency of an immediate ceasefire and the need to view the ceasefire as a major step towards a lasting political process and dialogue.
However, Maulvi Shahabuddin Dilawar, counsellor at the Taleban-controlled Afghan consulate in Peshawar, told AIP the attack on Bagram had been launched because the talks had failed.
"The Taleban held talks to show the people they also believe in talks, but regretted that there was no outcome," he said.

UNSMA said the talks had focused on implementing a ceasefire, forming a commission to supervise it, demilitarising Kabul, exchanging prisoners and creating conditions to establish a broad-based and fully representative government.
The Taleban hold more than two-thirds of Afghanistan and are battling opponents north of Kabul and in the remote northwest.
